entries.title: Complaints Against DOJ Officials Have Surged During Trump’s Second Term
entries.summary: The Office of Professional Responsibility has seen a 54% increase in misconduct complaints over the last two years, an inspector general report found.
entries.content:
Professional misconduct complaints against Department of Justice personnel have surged during President Donald Trump’s second term, according to an annual inspector general report documenting the department’s top challenges.

Tuesday’s findings from the department’s independent oversight office follow last year’s workforce reductions and a record-high caseload that includes dozens of lawsuits against the president’s political opponents.

The high number of complaints have led the department to open investigations into attorney misconduct, whistleblower retaliation and federal law enforcement conduct violations, the report says.

The DOJ’s Office of Professional Responsibility reported receiving 2,081 professional misconduct complaints last fiscal year, representing a 54% increase from 1,346 in 2024, the last full fiscal year during then-President Joe Biden’s administration, the report says.

The administration has been quickly outpacing DOJ complaints filed during Biden’s tenure, which were at their lowest in fiscal year 2023 at 1,085 recorded complaints, and their highest in 2024.

OPR found professional misconduct in each of the nine full-scale investigations that it completed this year, while one additional investigation has not yet been concluded, the report says. The office also received 50 new FBI whistleblower retaliation complaints.

The inspector general noted that the surge in misconduct complaints has put strain on the department’s shrinking workforce.

“These results demonstrate that OPR has continued to resolve substantial workloads despite its limited size,” the report states. “However, the Department faces risk in its oversight capacity if OPR’s staffing levels are insufficient to manage the workload generated by the Department’s thousands of employees.”

The review coincides with a record number of staff departures at the Department of Justice. The report cites a net decline of 10,345 department employees between January 2025 and May 2026.

Staffing levels are also impacting federal prosecutors’ ability to try cases across the country.

The report acknowledged concerns over the loss of critical expertise across the department, noting a 40% vacancy rate in the Missing or Murdered Indigenous Persons Regional Outreach Program and sprawling staffing issues in the Bureau of Prisons.

“Workforce reductions may produce mission degradation that aggregate staffing numbers do not reveal, particularly where departures are concentrated in specialized or difficult-to-replace positions,” the report warned.

entries.title: The Final Senate Race Is Called: Mary Peltola Flips Alaska Seat
entries.summary: The outcome of the race will give Democrats 56 seats in the Senate next year.
entries.content:
Mary Peltola is projected to win her race for U.S. Senate over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, locking in a Democratic Senate majority in which the party will hold 56 seats.

Alaska was the final Senate race left to be called, and took two weeks to conclude: On Tuesday evening, Peltola broke a majority of votes cast, meaning the contest didn’t require additional ranked-choice tabulations.

The weeks leading up to and after the election were marked by a flurry of legal activity around the contest.

Less than two weeks out from Election Day, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit that teed up a legal challenge to a possible Peltola victory. The lawsuit against Alaska election officials argued that they should not certify any outcome “that may be impacted by voter confusion” between Sen. Sullivan, the incumbent, and Daniel J. Sullivan, another candidate who appeared on the four-person ballot, without an investigation.

A federal judge dismissed the lawsuit, which was widely panned as a nonstarter by legal experts, the Sunday before Election Day. Democrats, including Peltola’s campaign, condemned the federal lawsuit but weren’t the only ones: Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska said the Justice Department “should never have filed this lawsuit,” in a clear break from her Republican peers.

The DOJ’s lawsuit divided Alaska’s state officials, too: While Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy said he would not commit to certifying the race results if there was uncertainty about the outcome, attorneys for Alaska election officials argued in a filing that a federal challenge to certifying the results has “no legal basis.” The chief officer of the Alaska Division of Elections is Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom, a Republican.

Just a week before Election Day, The New York Times reported that the Peltola campaign and national Democrats had plotted to recruit spoiler candidates to siphon votes from Sen. Sullivan — including Daniel J. Sullivan, the subject of the legal battle between the DOJ and Alaska election officials. Both the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee denied involvement in the recruitment to The Washington Sun.

The New York Times’ reporting bolstered the DOJ’s legal challenge — attorneys filed an amended complaint drawing on the evidence of the plan a few days later. The news also prompted backlash from Republicans toward Democrats: President Donald Trump said in a Truth Social post that Peltola should face legal and political consequences. Three investigations kicked off days after the news broke: Alaska’s governor ordered state officials to look into the plot, House Republicans announced a probe and the DOJ sent target letters to several people involved.

Some prominent Democrats defended the Peltola campaign, and national Democrats including Maryland Rep. Jamie Raskin said candidate recruitment is a common campaign tactic. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) called the plan to recruit other candidates “pretty dumb” but also highlighted that the actions aren’t illegal, and that it “happens in every election.”

Although Murkowski criticized the DOJ’s lawsuit, she also called the reported plot “simply wrong.”

In the days after the election, Trump posted on Truth Social, arguing that votes for Daniel J. Sullivan and the fourth candidate should be counted for Sen. Sullivan, citing potential confusion on the part of voters, and calling the race “rigged.”

A separate lawsuit also kicked off after Election Day.

As part of Alaska’s tabulation process, ballots are reviewed and can be rejected if election officials find voter information invalid or questionable. Peltola’s campaign sued the Alaska Division of Elections on Nov. 7, seeking to force the government to reveal the names of voters whose absentee ballots were rejected, but a state judge dismissed this new lawsuit four days later.

The state judge told the campaign that its request was “unreasonable” given the limited time for election officials to tabulate ballots.

Peltola’s win marks a striking shift in the state given that Trump won Alaska by 13 percentage points in 2024 — the same year Peltola lost her at-large congressional seat to Republican Rep. Nick Begich.

The Alaska Senate race was a competitive one, with the affordability crisis and Iran war on voters’ minds. Peltola focused on an “Alaska First” message and hammered Trump’s handling of the economy and foreign affairs, especially the president’s hostility toward Canada. Peltola, who is a Yup’ik Alaska Native, will be the first Alaska Native U.S. senator.

The Democrat also got a boost from a national political environment that soured on Trump and Republicans more broadly.

“She fixed the campaign on Alaskan issues versus hyperpartisan national issues,” said John-Henry Heckendorn, a Democratic strategist. “That’s allowed her to pull together a coalition across party lines that could actually compete with MAGA.”
entries.author: Ellie Fivas

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: Lack of Awareness
entries.content:
DSC02879.jpg (6000x3376, AR: 1.78)Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro Newsletter for Nov. 18, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: Emergency alerts, D.C. landlords and Tom Sietsema’s tips for holiday hosting. 

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 8/10. We’ll keep the brilliant sunshine of the past two days, and add several degrees to get us solidly into the 60s. That’s good stuff! Read the full forecast.





THE LATEST

D.C. Council members are pressing the Bowser administration about the timing of emergency alerts during last week’s active shooter situation in Logan Circle.

While first responders arrived almost instantly, The Sun’s Martin Austermuhle and Jenny Gathright report that it took far longer for nearby residents to get cellphone notifications about the situation — or any indication that the shooter could still be active.

Residents reported to D.C. Council member Elissa Silverman that it took until about 8:45 a.m. for them to get a text message from the AlertDC system — and the message, according to a screenshot posted on X, did not give residents any detail beyond alerting them to a shooting investigation in the area.

Martin and Jenny, who were both near the scene that morning, received wireless emergency alerts urging them to head indoors and shelter in place at 9 a.m. That was an hour after the first Fire and EMS dispatch to the shooting, and at least 55 minutes after first responders had been advised via radio that the shooter could still be at large and there were multiple victims, according to The Sun’s review of archived public radio chatter.

“It’s not acceptable,” said D.C. Council member Brooke Pinto, who represents the area where the shooting occurred and chairs the council’s public safety committee. “The reason we have the alert system is to make sure the public is aware when there’s a public safety emergency.”

Spokespeople for D.C.’s Homeland Security and Emergency Management Agency, which is in charge of issuing such alerts, did not provide a specific reason for the delay but told The Sun that the city is committed to providing “clear, timely public communication.”




FROM THE DISTRICT

DSC02879.jpg (6000x3376, AR: 1.78)
D.C. landlords are calling the police on tenant organizers, Ben Lauren writes for The Sun. Barring notices have long been an informal tool landlords use to keep potential safety risks to their properties at bay; someone who shows up in violation of one can be arrested. But since the start of 2025, organizers and residents say, the notices have been used to curb their efforts at improving conditions in some of the city’s most notorious properties.

Stuck in neutral: Metro hasn’t yet figured out how to fund the Gold Line, the rapid-transit bus line planned to get fans to the new Commanders stadium along the troubled H Street corridor, The Sun’s Zara Norman reports. The project has just $5 million of the $80 million to $85 million needed for construction. It’ll have to find the rest by spring 2027 if buses are to run in time for the stadium’s 2030 opening.

D.C. is throwing a $10 million lifeline to the Cedar Hill Regional Medical Center in Ward 8, looking to sustain its money-losing labor-and-delivery unit, The Sun’s Martin Austermuhle reports. The hospital — which was built with $434 million in public funds — has struggled to find its footing since it opened in April 2025, but city leaders are loath to let it flounder since it provides needed health services for some of D.C.’s lowest-income neighborhoods.

Nearly a week after a D.C. Council hearing on truancy, the city’s education leaders continue to debate who, or what, is to blame for the issue, The Sun’s Shamira Muhammad reports. Washington Teacher’s Union President Laura Fuchs testified that D.C.’s system of school choice has drawn financial resources away from public schools, which have inherited a greater percentage of the “students who require the most support and therefore need greater investment.”

In a statement Tuesday, D.C. Charter School Alliance Executive Director Ariel Johnson pushed back, arguing that nearly half of D.C. students attend charter schools. “School leaders and educators in DCPS and public charter schools alike are doing extraordinary work under real pressure, and they deserve partners, not blame,” Johnson said.





FROM VIRGINIA

Space race: Virginia and Maryland have both submitted bids to host the proposed U.S. Space Academy, Axios D.C. reports. The academy, launched by President Donald Trump this year, would function like U.S. military academies and train cadets for the Space Force, NASA and private spaceflight.

They’re hoping some NASA nepotism might sweeten the bid. Virginia proposed hosting it on 600 acres across NASA’s Langley Research Center and Fort Monroe in Hampton, with a satellite campus at NASA’s Wallops Flight Facility. Maryland is eyeing the University of Maryland until it can host in Greenbelt near NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center, The Banner reports.





FROM MARYLAND

The Rockville City Council approved a resolution to lower the voting age in municipal elections from 18 to 16. Supporters say the change will help drive youth civic engagement, but residents largely voted down the same proposal on a ballot question three years ago, The Sun’s Justice Covert reports.

A slate of top cop nominations in Montgomery County has ruffled feathers as some officials question how, less than two weeks after being elected county executive, Will Jawando made his picks. Jawando has called for confirmations to happen before the council breaks for the holidays, but council member Dawn Luedtke told The Sun’s Emma Ruby that the open positions are being filled on an interim basis — so why the rush?





FROM THE DINING ROOM

Are you a veteran host who wants to up your game? Perhaps you’re a newbie in search of inspiration, or you simply wish to be a great house guest.

In any case, Tom Sietsema has you covered. Hospitality experts tell The Sun’s food correspondent that you should clean your house — yup, including your fridge — when hosting, stock up on take-home boxes and never forget to queue some good music. If you’re a guest, bring a token of appreciation.

“When you’re a guest, act like a host, and when you’re a host, act like a guest,” says Amanda McClements, the owner of the chic Salt & Sundry lifestyle boutiques in Washington.





PLAN YOUR WEEKEND

Zoo lights (8192x5464, AR: 1.50)For the whole family: Zoo Lights at the National Zoo, Friday through Jan. 3.

For Hamilton heads: Mandy Gonzalez sings Lin-Manuel Miranda at Strathmore, Friday.

For CGI haters: “Labyrinth” with a live band at the Lincoln Theatre, Sunday.

For more info on this weekend’s events, read our weekly culture calendar here.





SPORTS

Is Georgetown basketball back? The Hoyas have a chance to move to 5-0 tonight as they host Navy. Coach Ed Cooley’s team already has early wins against Maryland and Clemson under its belt, thanks in part to some stellar additions from the transfer portal. The Sun’s Alex Schiffer reports that neither Cooley nor his players are overhyping the hot start — the Hoyas started 5-0 a year ago but ended the season at 16-18. But the team is hoping this success will help fill Capitol One Arena.

“It’s not so much who we’re playing — come cheer for us,” Cooley said. “We could be playing against the circus. Let’s cheer against those clowns.”

The Nationals did some more roster shuffling Tuesday, adding four players to the 40-man roster and removing four others to make room, The Sun’s Jesse Dougherty writes. Three of the four players added — Jarlin Susana, Travis Sykora and Alejandro Rosario, all right-handed pitchers — are now protected from being taken by another team in the Rule 5 Draft this winter (which is scheduled for December but could be delayed or even canceled because of the expected work stoppage).

The four pitchers designated for assignment to clear space included fan favorite Josiah Gray, who returned this September after more than two years of rehabbing his elbow.

What to Watch Today

NCAAW: Maryland vs. Coppin State, 6 p.m. (B1G+)

NCAAM: Georgetown vs. Navy, 6:30 p.m. (ESPN+)

NBA: Wizards at Raptors, 7:30 p.m. (Monumental)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@washsun.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson

entries.title: Iran Targets a U.S. Base in Kuwait
entries.summary: The attacks, including ones on Bahrain, appear to be retaliation for American strikes on Tuesday.
entries.content:
By David Rising and Samy Magdy

Iran widened its attacks on its Gulf neighbors on Wednesday, targeting a U.S. air base in Kuwait and launching several attacks on Bahrain in what appeared to be retaliation for American strikes the day before.

After about two months without such attacks, Iran has repeatedly targeted U.S. facilities in Bahrain in recent days. The small Persian Gulf island kingdom hosts the U.S. Navy’s 5th Fleet.

The early morning attacks came after a U.S. fighter jet struck a Revolutionary Guard missile launch site Tuesday on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. strike was in retaliation for an Iranian attack on an American radar installation in Bahrain earlier Tuesday.

Iran said that its recent attacks — including those on other U.S. facilities in Bahrain on Sunday and Friday — were in response to U.S. drone surveillance operations and an attack on Iranian communications towers.

The uptick in fighting with the tit-for-tat attacks raises the risk of further escalation toward the resumption of all-out conflict nearly nine months into the war, and complicates negotiations for a diplomatic solution, which have stagnated despite intensified mediation efforts from Qatar.

The U.S. military didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on the latest attacks.

With its economy suffering under a U.S. naval blockade and American military escorts helping restore the passage of oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz, experts say that the recent attacks suggest Tehran may be growing weary of the status quo.

“Even if neither side intends to enter a broader confrontation, the accumulation of military incidents across multiple fronts increases the risk of miscalculation and escalation beyond what either side originally intended,” Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group think tank, wrote in an analysis posted to X following the initial reports of the attack on Kuwait.

U.S. President Donald Trump has sent mixed messages on his next steps, saying new strikes are highly unlikely, but also sending a third aircraft carrier and thousands more troops to the Middle East.

Though U.S. military protection has helped restore oil shipments from the Gulf, Iran has continued to attack tankers as they attempt to transit the Strait of Hormuz.

United Arab Emirates state-owned oil company ADNOC said Wednesday that one of its tanker crew members was missing after an attack in the strait on Tuesday, while 11 others were injured and were receiving medical care.

entries.title: The Trump Administration Is Fighting to Keep Freezing Solar Program Grants
entries.summary: The administration is appealing a decision that it illegally froze Solar for All funds.
entries.content:
The Trump administration is appealing a court ruling that it illegally froze funds for a nationwide solar program, thrusting grant recipients into more uncertainty.

The $7 billion Solar for All program was created to make solar power accessible to lower-income communities. More than 30 states and organizations received awards before the Environmental Protection Agency halted the program in August 2025.

Those awards have been in limbo for the past year. In court filings, groups suing the EPA said solar companies and nonprofits have had to shift their focus, in some cases forcing major layoffs of workers hired to help with Solar for All programming.

In September, two federal judges ruled in separate cases that the Trump administration’s termination of the program was illegal. Those rulings did not require federal officials to immediately disburse funds to grantees.

Adam Kent, senior director of green finance at the Natural Resources Defense Council, said the program drew enthusiasm from both sides of the aisle, and a continued funding freeze would threaten affordability.

“Skyrocketing utility bills are putting a squeeze on Americans from Anchorage to Orlando, but the Trump administration is ignoring their plight. Instead of getting out of the way of a program that will lower energy bills, the Trump administration is continuing its obstruction and delay,” he said in a statement.

Other cases involving Solar for All grants are moving forward in the Court of Federal Claims, where states and organizations can sue the federal government for damages over contract issues, but not for other kinds of relief like the reinstatement of programs. The Trump administration has argued that cases over its cancellation of Biden-era climate programs belong in that court, rather than in federal courts.
entries.author: Mara Hoplamazian

entries.title: Metro May Cut Bus Routes and Reduce Rail Service to Make Up Budget Gap
entries.summary: Metro is considering cutting frequency on 13 popular bus routes and reducing service on five metro rail lines.
entries.content:
The Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority is considering significant service reductions across bus and train lines to bridge a projected budget shortfall up to $132 million driven by skyrocketing fuel prices, inflation and less than anticipated subsidies from regional transit agencies.

To close the fiscal 2028 budget gap, Metro may cut frequency on 13 popular bus routes, stop 24-hour bus service and eliminate 10 lower ridership lines, according to documents released ahead of a Thursday meeting where Metro’s general manager will present a proposed operating budget. Metro could also reduce service on five of its six train lines and shorten weekend operating hours systemwide.

“Metro certainly wants to keep growing ridership & not cut service or have a significant fare increases, but the reality is we don’t have a dedicated predictable funding model that can absorb inflation impacts on electricity, Paratranist, diesel and labor,” Metro General Manager Randy Clarke said on social media in a response to the changes.

“We need DMVMoves approved,” he said, referring to a joint regional funding model for Metro that was endorsed by the Board of Directors last year but has yet to be funded by local municipalities. A key proposal of DMVMoves is $460 million in new annual capital funding to start in fiscal 2028.

Metro has struggled in recent years to stay in the green. The agency relies on subsidies from various local authorities and fare revenue rather than a dedicated funding stream. Metro received more in subsidies this year than last year, but still less than an anticipated 3% hike. A spokesperson for Metro told The Washington Sun in a statement that dedicated funding from the DMVMoves initiative would help address long-standing budget concerns.

In the documents released this week, Metro said it needs more subsidies to prevent "significant impacts on system maintenance and improvements.” D.C. allocated $724 million to the transit agency in fiscal 25, making Metro one of the city’s highest operating budget expenditures. Still, the agency is hoping to garner more support from local agencies to avoid “major service cuts” that would “reduce its usefulness to customers and risk reversing positive ridership momentum.”

Metro said rising wage costs hit the budget hard this year as well as increasing fuel and energy prices. Diesel prices increased 70% compared with last year, and energy prices went up 20%, Metro said.

The agency proposed an 11% “inflation-based” fare increase in October to help balance the budget. An updated pitch could hike prices up 22%, up between $2.75 and $8.25, and bring in $85 million of revenue. The rail system would likely see 16 million fewer trips, Metro estimated.

Metro has long had problems with frequent fare evaders and estimated it loses $57 million annually to riders who don't pay to ride the bus. The agency tried to crack down on free riders earlier this year by requiring drivers to quote rates to each boarding customer but reversed course after pushback from worker unions. In documents released this week, Metro said varying fare evasion fines across the DMV challenge progress in increasing compliance.
Bus routes (2452x1030, AR: 2.38)Axing low ridership buses would decrease connectivity across the region as most proposed routes connect D.C. to Maryland or Virginia, cutting direct service and making travel times longer.

Reduced service on high ridership routes would push bus frequency from every 12-20 minutes to every 15-40 minutes, making buses more crowded and transit generally “less useful,” the board documents said. If the board approved each bus service reduction proposal, the agency would save $42.5 million but reduce overall ridership by 4.6 million trips.

Metro did not answer questions from The Sun about how likely the board is to approve each proposed money-saving option.

Cutting back Metrorail service would impose similar consequences as lessening buses — crowding rail cars, making customers wait longer for trains and reducing support for late-night travel.

The Orange, Silver and Blue Lines would always run every 15 minutes rather than the current 10-minute weekday and 12-minute weekend frequency. The Yellow Line would not run north of the Mount Vernon Square station, and only every other Red Line train would go to each end of the route, past Silver Spring and Grosvernor-Strathmore stations.

Train service would end earlier and start later on weekends, stopping at 1 a.m. on Fridays and Saturdays instead of the current 2 a.m. cutoff and beginning at 7 a.m on Saturdays and Sundays instead of 6 a.m.

The train service changes could save $37.2 million but would reduce ridership by 5.13 million trips, the board documents said.

entries.title: Musk Distances Himself From MAGA and Says He Regrets His Record Midterm Spending
entries.summary: Elon Musk spent nearly half a billion on a slate of congressional candidates, the majority of whom lost to Democratic opponents.
entries.content:
Elon Musk, the world’s richest man and an on-again, off-again ally of Donald Trump’s, attempted in a public interview to distance himself from the president’s MAGA movement and expressed regret for spending nearly $500 million in a doomed attempt to boost Republican candidates this election cycle.

The money did not appear to make much of a difference in this month’s midterms, which saw a wave of Democrats elected to office even in historically red states such as Texas, Kansas, Mississippi and Montana.

“I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it, or maybe it would have been much worse,” Musk told journalist Andrew Ross Sorkin while speaking at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit on Wednesday.

“It certainly shows that American elections are not just about money,” he continued. “If I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money.”

The Tesla and SpaceX chief executive spent big on Republican Senate races — particularly on Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s big loss to Sen.-elect James Talarico. He also bankrolled losing campaigns in Maine, Ohio, Michigan and Alaska.

Only three of the roughly 40 Republican House candidates Musk financed won at the polls, according to Reuters.
https://x.com/dealbook/status/2123189298849595422?a=dr_3MpgwUMgKkGzZJLE&s=20At the conference Wednesday, Musk also attempted to moderate his allegiance to Trump, saying “there are positives and negatives in both parties.”

“I’m not sure what MAGA means, but if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that,” he said.
entries.author: Gavin J. Quinton
